ledger.contribution: Studies robotic kinematics and motion planning in configuration space, applying geometric and computational reasoning. This is an application of mathematics; it does not supply the group-theoretic, projective/hyperbolic or topological course sequence.
ledger.actualProfile: Robotics is a broad interdisciplinary field that integrates computing science, mathematics, various branches of engineering, and, more recently, also knowledge from social sciences and humanities. In addition to introducing the participants to key notions and concepts in robotics and industrial automation, the course focuses on computational problems that arise in the field, in particular related to motion and manipulation, which are core abilities of an autonomous robot. Among the main topics that we address is kinematics, which studies motions of objects without taking the causes of these motions into account. Forward kinematics considers the relation between the configuration of the joints of a robotic arm and the position and orientation of the tip (or tool, hand, or end effector) of the arm. Inverse kinematics tackles the problem of configuring and controlling the joints of the arm in such a way that the tip can accomplish a given task. We also study motion or path planning, where the goal is to find a path for an autonomous robot from an initial to a final placement while avoiding collisions with the obstacles in its environment. We will learn how to translate the motion planning problem into a problem in so-called configuration space, and then study the structure of that space. We distinguish exact and approximate approaches to solving the problem. Exact approaches guarantee to find a path whenever one exists but are generally complex and only work for simple instances of the problem.
ledger.actualDescription: Covers computational problems in robotics. Includes forward and inverse kinematics, motion planning, collision avoidance and robotic grasping and manipulation.

ledger.actualProfile: Linear algebra is the study of systems of linear equations and linear functions. Systematic methods exist to solve such systems of linear equations. Matrices and vectors are introduced as the equivalent of a system of linear equations. This equivalence allows for reducing problems involving linear combinations of vectors to questions about systems of linear equations. The spanning of a (sub)space, linear independence and linear transformations are fundamental concepts in linear algebra. Matrix operations and theorems involving matrices will provide the basic tools for handling many applications of linear algebra. The invertible matrix theorem is a theorem of particular importance. The determinant of a matrix is an important scalar quantity related to the invertibility criterion for square matrices. Furthermore, the determinant is a measure for the amount by which a linear transformation changes the area of a ﬁgure. In multi-variable calculus, this measure is deﬁned as the Jacobian of a transformation. Introducing the more abstract concept of vector spaces allows for further generalization of these ideas. Many vector spaces resemble the well-known vector space Rn. In this course, the theory of vector spaces will be applied to the processing of discrete signals (Fourier Series), diﬀerence equations and Markov chains. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors are used to understand the action of a linear transformation. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors arise naturally in diﬀerent areas of physics and mathematics.

The prerequisite gateway courseMathematical Methods introduces techniques and methods for solving equations in one variable, for finding derivatives of func- tions, or for solving integrals,etc., analytically. Numerical solutions obtained through some al- gorithm pose the following challenge: what does the output mean? How sensitive is the algorithm to a wrong input? Numerical and computational mathematics is a broad topic; numerous algorithms exist for numerically solving the same mathematical problem. This courses focuses on algorithms for solving equations in one variable. Numerical methods for differentiation, but especially integration form a set of very important numerical algorithms. ledger.actualProfile: The concepts of signals and systems appear in a wide variety of fields. The physical nature of the sig- nals to be acquired and the measurement systems may differ from application to application, but they all have in common that the signals contain information about the observed phenomenon and secondly, the systems respond to particular signals by producing other signals or certain behavior as output. This course discusses how to characterize alinear time-invariant systemand how it will respond to var- ious inputs. Theunit-impulse responseor - its equivalent in the frequency domain - thefrequency responsecharacterizes a linear time-invariant system. This course discussesconvolution. TheFourier series representationrepresents periodic signals as infinite harmonic series in continuous time and finite harmonic series in discrete time. Increasing the period of the periodic signals amounts to a denser Fourier series representation. In the limiting case that the period becomes infinitely long, the Fourier series rep- resentation becomes theFourier transform- both in continuous-time and in discrete-time. The course discusses the properties of the Fourier series representation and the Fourier transform in great detail. A very important characteristic of the Fourier transform is the duality property. TheLaplace transform generalizes the Fourier transform for continuous-time signals. In a very similar way, theZ-transform generalizes the Fourier transform for discrete-time signals.

ledger.actualProfile: Ecology is the scientific study of the distribution and abundance of organisms and the interactions that determine distribution and abundance. Over the past decades, ecology has grown from an obscure science into a position at the forefront of public and political consciousness. Applied ecology has become an important scientific tool to address important political and environmental issues. Ecology is generally divided into 3 levels: the individual organism, the population (consisting of individuals of the same species) and the community, in which several species are living together. In addition, ecology focuses on the relationship between living creatures and their chemical and physical surroundings, which together make up an ecosystem. Ecology is a complex science. It draws on many areas of knowledge such as organic and inorganic chemistry, plant and animal biology, physiology, meteorology, and even economics. This course focuses on the basic principles of ecology, from individuals to ecosystems. We then proceed to environmental conditions and resources, and the 4 levels of ecology: individuals, populations, communities and ecosystems. Two weeks will be spent on ecological modelling, as an important tool for understanding and predicting ecological systems. We will conclude with some actual cases of applied ecology.

ledger.contribution: examines the nature of knowledge and the theoretical methods philosophers use to support conclusions, including the relation of philosophy to physics and computer science, the philosophical reflection on scientific knowledge that the core's philosophy component addresses
ledger.actualProfile: Philosophy asks the most fundamental questions about the ways we think and act—about, amongst other things, the nature of knowledge, consciousness, our responsibilities towards others, freedom, the existence of god, whether and in what sense our lives can be said to have meaning. Philosophical questions might appear to be simple at first glance, and many of us would have immediate intuitive responses to at least some of them. But providing coherent, lucid, and compelling responses to philosophical questions is a very challenging endeavor. This course introduces central themes from the Western philosophical tradition, spanning 2,500 years of history from the ancient Greeks to cutting-edge work from our own time. We will become familiar with the issues discussed by philosophers, inquire into their significance and their relation to thought in other disciplines, such as psychology, law, physics, computer science, and political science. And, even more importantly, we will acquaint ourselves with theoretical methods and tools that have been used by philosophers to support their conclusions and ideas. 3 Through detailed engagement with central philosophical ideas and arguments, we will develop a critical perspective and approach the rewarding task of articulating our own views on philosophical issues. We shall see that philosophy is a paradigmatic exercise in critical reasoning: it provides an opportunity to develop reasoning skills through rigorous and precise argumentation concerning issues of great importance to our lives.

ledger.contribution: develops the main ethical theories and applies them to practical questions, the ethics component of the core
ledger.actualProfile: Our actions and decisions are structured by the ways we think about values, about what the good is. This course explores theories of moral reasoning, building upon historical and contemporary sources. In the first part of the course, we will examine the main theories in ethics – virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism – as well as questions pertaining to moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility, feminist contributions to ethical theory, the challenge of nihilism, and the relation of happiness and pleasure to ethics. The second part of the course largely focuses on practical ethics, touching upon topics such as equality, animal rights, poverty and wealth, future generations, climate change, historical injustice. We will examine our attitudes to these contentious and challenging issues, the way the topics relate to each other, and the manner in which questions in practical ethics highlight and bring into focus broader concerns pertaining to moral, political, and legal theory. Students taking the course will acquire in-depth knowledge of ethical theories, to be assessed through a mid-term exam. They will also work on developing research skills in papers and presentations, analyzing and assessing arguments from ethical theory and practical ethics while articulating an independent, informed perspective. Towards that end, throughout the term students will compose two reflection papers concerning topics in ethics, and in the second part of the term students will develop a research project comprising a final argumentative essay and a presentation.

Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.

ledger.contribution: Develops critical appraisal of evidence about disease, risk and population change. This is a complementary empirical setting; the actual profile does not document mathematical epidemic models or optimisation.
ledger.actualProfile: Public health is about changing the world. From pandemics to lifestyle-related diseases, from screening for disease to improving water and air quality, it asks: how can we improve to keep the population healthy?_x000D_ But how do we know what actually works? In this course you will dive into epidemiology: the science behind public health. You will learn how to study disease, risks, and changes over time, and how to critically evaluate evidence. Because behind every public health decision lies a question of evidence, and by the end of this course, you will be equipped to engage with it. This course invites you to look beyond the lab, the hospital, and the library, into the wider world where health is shaped. What matters most if we truly care about health, and how can we influence that?

ledger.contribution: develops multivariate statistical models, including linear and logistic regression, factor analysis, analysis of covariance and non-parametric tests, extending statistical inference to models with many variables
ledger.actualProfile: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in in medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers whether in data science, business analytics, market research, political science or sociology. The phenomena investigated by scientists studying humans are usually complex, thus multiple variables must be used to explain them. The theory and application of multivariate statistical models will be discussed. These models can be used to investigate the relations among many variables simultaneously, thus providing an accurate explanation of the subject of interest. The course introduces most used multivariate statistical models such as linear regression, factor analysis, analysis of (co)variance, and logistic regression. Furthermore, attention is paid to non-parametric tests. Practical application: you will learn to apply these models to data. In addition, learn how to deal with problems that occur when statistical models are used. At the end of the course, you will be able to determine which statistical model should be used to investigate different types of research questions. Furthermore, you will be able to execute the corresponding analyses and report results, conforming to APA guidelines.
